title: Short-lived access with a Vault-signed SSH CA
summary: Per-role SSH through short-lived certificates instead of static keys and shared sudo grants.

stat.label: every certificate expires on its own; revocation is the clock

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: Static SSH keys and shared sudo grants give every session more access than its task needs.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: Before this, the deploy roles shared one static key. I chose Vault-signed certificates over a directory service, an LDAP proxy and per-role static keys.

Vault holds the CA private key and it never leaves. A caller sends its public key to a signing role and gets back a certificate that names one principal and expires with the role. A host trusts the CA and lists, per local user, which principals may log in as that user. Hosts verify certificates offline, so no host calls Vault. A time-limited break-glass path covers admin work.

sections.heading: Result so far
paragraphs: Phase 1 shipped as one PR, then follow-up PRs through the normal flow that fixed the role and its checks, such as revoking principals files the role does not own and not reloading sshd on hosts that start it by socket.

Each signing role names one principal and one lifetime: an hour at most for admin work, less for the service that reads the inventory. Revocation is the clock, not a list. Nothing is signed while Vault is sealed, so a scheduled caller fails loudly. Since 18 November Vault opens itself through AWS KMS, so a seal is rare.
The role adds certificate trust beside the keys a host already has and never removes a static key. The rollout goes one canary host at a time, and no host has dropped its static keys.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: A sudo grant belongs to the user ID, not the process, so isolation must be designed at the identity level.
